Comparison with VisCollin

Source: vignettes/articles/comparison-viscollin.Rmd
comparison-viscollin.Rmd

Why this comparison

VisCollin (Friendly, n.d.) is the reference R implementation of the Belsley-Kuh-Welsch collinearity diagnostics (Belsley et al. 1980) and of their graphical display (tableplots and collinearity biplots) proposed by Friendly and Kwan (2009). It works on lm and glm objects, so it is the natural point of comparison for multiCollglm. This article answers three questions on real data:

  1. What exactly does VisCollin::colldiag() compute when it is given a GLM?
  2. Does multiCollglm reproduce it, and with which setting?
  3. Where do the two give different answers, and why?

The short answers are: colldiag() decomposes the original design matrix and ignores the family, the link and the IRLS weights, which is exactly multiCollglm’s method = "X"; the two coincide to machine precision there; and they differ whenever the information matrix \(X'\hat W X\) is not proportional to \(X'X\), which is the usual case in a GLM.

library(multiCollglm)
library(VisCollin)

# TEMP of the Lee data is stored on a /100 scale; multiply it back by 100
lee <- LeeCancer
lee$x6100 <- lee$x6 * 100

mods <- list(
  Lee      = glm(y ~ x1 + x4 + x6100, family = binomial(), data = lee),
  Nitrogen = glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, family = Gamma(link = "inverse"),
                 data = Nitrogen),
  Mine     = glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, family = poisson(), data = Mine),
  Plastic  = glm(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4, family = poisson(), data = Plastic)
)

What colldiag() does with a GLM

The relevant lines of colldiag() are (VisCollin 0.1.4):

X <- mod$model[, -1]                 # drop the response from the model frame
X <- na.omit(X)
if (add.intercept) X <- cbind(1, X)  # default: FALSE
X <- scale(X, scale = scale, center = center)
svdX <- svd(X)

So, for a glm, it takes the columns of the model frame, optionally adds a column of ones, scales them (by default, dividing each column by its root-mean-square, without centering) and takes the SVD. The fitted model itself is never used: no family, no link, no IRLS weights. Its defaults (add.intercept = FALSE) reproduce SAS PROC REG ... COLLINNOINT, following the argument of Fox (1997) that diagnostics including the intercept are only meaningful when it has a real interpretation.

Dividing by the root-mean-square instead of by the Euclidean norm multiplies every column by the same constant, \(\sqrt{n-1}\), so condition indices and variance proportions are the same as with unit-length columns.

Where they coincide: method = "X"

With add.intercept = TRUE, colldiag() and bkw_diagnostics(method = "X") decompose the same matrix, \(X_{ul}'X_{ul}\) (original design matrix, unit length, intercept included, no weights). For the four datasets of the package:

same <- sapply(mods, function(m) {
  cd <- colldiag(m, add.intercept = TRUE)
  bk <- bkw_diagnostics(m, method = "X")
  c(
    max_diff_condition_index = max(abs(cd$condindx[, 1] - bk$condition_index)),
    # colldiag() stores components in rows; multiCollglm in columns
    max_diff_proportions     = max(abs(t(cd$pi) - bk$proportions))
  )
})
t(same)
#>          max_diff_condition_index max_diff_proportions
#> Lee                  3.584546e-10         5.719730e-14
#> Nitrogen             1.833200e-11         1.301181e-13
#> Mine                 8.171241e-14         3.996803e-15
#> Plastic              3.634796e-09         4.498291e-12

The differences are floating-point noise: condition indices and proportions agree to at least ten significant digits. The same holds for the colldiag() default (no intercept) when the GLM is fitted without intercept:

m_noint <- update(mods$Mine, . ~ . - 1)
c(colldiag    = max(colldiag(m_noint)$condindx),
  multiCollglm = condition_number(m_noint, method = "X")$condition_index)
#>     colldiag multiCollglm 
#>     6.402271     6.402271

Hence the one-line translation table:

VisCollin multiCollglm
colldiag(mod, add.intercept = TRUE) bkw_diagnostics(mod, method = "X")
colldiag(mod) (no intercept, the default) bkw_diagnostics(<mod fitted without intercept>, method = "X")
colldiag(mod, center = TRUE) not available (centering is deliberately not offered)
largest condition index condition_number(mod, method = "X")$condition_index

Where they differ (1): the IRLS weights

In a GLM the precision of \(\hat\beta\) is governed by the information matrix \(X'\hat W X\), not by \(X'X\). When the weights \(\hat W\) are not constant, the collinearity of the regressors (what colldiag() measures) and the conditioning of the information matrix (what the default method = "WS" measures) are different things. For the same models:

cn <- function(m) {
  c(`VisCollin (colldiag)` = max(colldiag(m, add.intercept = TRUE)$condindx),
    sapply(c(WS = "WS", MP = "MP", X = "X", RAW = "RAW"),
           function(k) condition_number(m, method = k)$condition_index))
}
knitr::kable(t(sapply(mods, cn)), digits = 4,
             caption = "sqrt(CN) on the same data; the VisCollin column equals method X.")
sqrt(CN) on the same data; the VisCollin column equals method X.
VisCollin (colldiag) WS MP X RAW
Lee 190.7765 315.1366 329.9542 190.7765 10808.133
Nitrogen 67.7053 77.9772 75.9081 67.7053 8790.650
Mine 19.8950 28.5822 26.4538 19.8950 2093.316
Plastic 595.7429 876.8393 899.0447 595.7429 73561.624

For these four applications the weighted definitions are larger than the unweighted one (Lee: 190.78 with colldiag(), 315.14 with "WS"; Plastic: 595.74 against 876.84), so a diagnostic that ignores the weights understates the ill-conditioning of the estimation problem. In other applications the difference may go the other way, or vanish; what matters is that it cannot be known without computing the weighted version.

The same happens with the variance-decomposition proportions. For the Lee model both approaches single out the intercept and TEMP (x6100) in the largest dimension, but with the weights a third dimension becomes problematic as well (sqrt(CN) 31.96, against 11.80 with colldiag()), and the proportions of the other dimensions are distributed differently:

print(colldiag(mods$Lee, add.intercept = TRUE), fuzz = 0.3)
#> Condition
#> Index    Variance Decomposition Proportions
#>            intercept x1    x4    x6100
#> 1    1.000  .         .     .     .   
#> 2    5.448  .         .    0.979  .   
#> 3   11.799  .        0.969  .     .   
#> 4  190.776 0.999      .     .    0.999
bkw <- bkw_diagnostics(mods$Lee)            # method = "WS"
bkw
#> Collinearity diagnostics (Belsley-Kuh-Welsch) on (X'WX)_ul [method = "WS"]
#> 
#>      Eigenvalue Sing.value sqrt(CN)
#> dim1      3.903      1.976    1.000
#> dim2      0.093      0.305    6.488
#> dim3      0.004      0.062   31.958
#> dim4      0.000      0.006  315.137
#> 
#> Variance-decomposition proportions (row = coefficient, column = component):
#>              dim1  dim2  dim3  dim4
#> (Intercept) 0.000 0.000 0.005 0.995
#> x1          0.000 0.007 0.817 0.176
#> x4          0.003 0.457 0.095 0.444
#> x6100       0.000 0.000 0.003 0.997
#> 
#> >> Possible collinearity problems (sqrt(CN) >= 10 and proportion >= 0.5 on >= 2 variables):
#>   - dim4 (sqrt(CN) = 315.14): (Intercept), x6100

When the weights are constant everything coincides

If \(\hat W\) is a multiple of the identity, weighting does nothing and the three scaled definitions collapse into the one of colldiag(). That is the case for a Gaussian model with identity link (the linear model):

m_gauss <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, family = gaussian(), data = Mine)
c(colldiag = max(colldiag(m_gauss, add.intercept = TRUE)$condindx),
  sapply(c("WS", "MP", "X"),
         function(k) condition_number(m_gauss, method = k)$condition_index))
#> colldiag       WS       MP        X 
#> 19.89504 19.89504 19.89504 19.89504

and, less obviously, for a Gamma model with log link, whose IRLS weights are identically 1 (see the Bodyfat article):

data("bodyfat", package = "TH.data")
m_body <- glm(DEXfat ~ age + waistcirc + hipcirc + elbowbreadth + kneebreadth +
                anthro3a + anthro3b + anthro3c + anthro4,
              family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = bodyfat)
range(m_body$weights)
#> [1] 1 1
c(colldiag = max(colldiag(m_body, add.intercept = TRUE)$condindx),
  sapply(c("WS", "MP", "X"),
         function(k) condition_number(m_body, method = k)$condition_index))
#> colldiag       WS       MP        X 
#> 352.0413 352.0413 352.0413 352.0413

Where they differ (2): the model frame

Because colldiag() reads mod$model[, -1], what it analyses is whatever sits in the model frame, not the design matrix the model was fitted with. Two consequences, both easy to hit in a GLM:

Prior weights and offsets are treated as regressors. A model fitted with weights = (very common for binomial or Poisson-rate models) stores the weights in the model frame as a column called (weights), which then enters the diagnostic as if it were an explanatory variable:

set.seed(2)
d <- Mine
d$w <- runif(nrow(d), 1, 3)
m_w <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = poisson(), data = d, weights = w)

colnames(colldiag(m_w, add.intercept = TRUE)$pi)   # VisCollin
#> [1] "intercept" "x1"        "x2"        "(weights)"
rownames(bkw_diagnostics(m_w, method = "X")$proportions)  # multiCollglm
#> [1] "(Intercept)" "x1"          "x2"

Factors are not expanded. multiCollglm works on model.matrix(mod) (dummy variables, interactions, polynomial terms included), whereas colldiag() receives the raw factor:

d$f <- factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), length.out = nrow(d)))
m_f <- glm(y ~ x1 + f, family = poisson(), data = d)

res <- try(colldiag(m_f, add.intercept = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
cat(if (inherits(res, "try-error")) res else "no error")
#> Error in v^2 : non-numeric argument to binary operator
rownames(bkw_diagnostics(m_f, method = "X")$proportions)
#> [1] "(Intercept)" "x1"          "fb"          "fc"          "fd"

(With colldiag() the usual work-around is to pass model.matrix(mod)[, -1] as a matrix instead of the model.)

Where they differ (3): visualization

VisCollin has what multiCollglm does not: the tableplot and the collinearity biplot of Friendly and Kwan (2009). multiCollglm returns tables only. The two are not exclusive: the tableplot only needs a list with the condition indices and the proportions, so it can be drawn from a GLM-aware decomposition by wrapping it in a colldiag object:

as_colldiag <- function(bkw) {
  ci <- matrix(bkw$condition_index, ncol = 1,
               dimnames = list(seq_along(bkw$condition_index), "cond.index"))
  structure(list(condindx = ci, pi = t(bkw$proportions)), class = "colldiag")
}
tableplot(colldiag(mods$Mine, add.intercept = TRUE),
          title = "VisCollin::colldiag (original X)")
tableplot(as_colldiag(bkw_diagnostics(mods$Mine)),
          title = "multiCollglm, method = \"WS\"")

Left: collinearity of the regressors. Right: conditioning of the information matrix of the Poisson model. In the Mine model both point to the intercept and x2 in the last dimension, but the weighted version reaches a larger condition index (28.6 against 19.9).

A caveat on the tool itself: in the version used here (0.1.4), tableplot() fails with an error when a variance proportion rounds to 100 (for instance with the Lee data), because of how the colour classes are cut; this is why the Mine data are used for the plots.

Summary

VisCollin multiCollglm
Model classes lm, glm (as a model frame), matrices glm, glmnet, cv.glmnet
Uses family, link and IRLS weights No Yes ("WS", "MP", "RAW"); no with "X"
Original design matrix, unit length Yes (scale = TRUE) method = "X"
Intercept Excluded by default (add.intercept) Always included (detects non-essential collinearity)
Centering center = TRUE Not offered
Design matrix model frame (factors, (weights), offsets not handled) model.matrix()
Condition index and BKW proportions Yes Yes (same numbers for method = "X")
RVIF (Salmerón et al. 2025) and ML-collinearity (Lesaffre and Marx 1993) No Yes
Regularized fits (glmnet) No Yes (refit on the active set)
Tableplot and collinearity biplot Yes No (tableplot can be drawn from bkw_diagnostics(), see above)

In practice: for a linear model, or to look at the collinearity among the regressors themselves, VisCollin and multiCollglm(method = "X") are interchangeable, and VisCollin adds the graphics. For a GLM, the default method = "WS" is the diagnostic of the matrix that actually determines the precision of the estimates.

Reproducibility

The comparison was run with the code of VisCollin 0.1.4 (GitHub version); the version installed when this page is built is shown below. The only functions of VisCollin used are colldiag() and tableplot().

References

Belsley, D. A., E. Kuh, and R. E. Welsch. 1980. Regression Diagnostics: Identifying Influential Data and Sources of Collinearity. Wiley.
Fox, J. 1997. Applied Regression Analysis, Linear Models, and Related Methods. Sage.
Friendly, M. n.d. VisCollin: Visualizing Collinearity Diagnostics. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=VisCollin.
Friendly, M., and E. Kwan. 2009. “Where’s Waldo: Visualizing Collinearity Diagnostics.” The American Statistician 63 (1): 56–65. https://doi.org/10.1198/tast.2009.0012.
Lesaffre, E., and B. D. Marx. 1993. “Collinearity in Generalized Linear Regression.” Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods 22 (7): 1933–52. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610929308831126.
